[MUJAHID:v1p368#2/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · author | holds | Turning away and leaning aside means becoming distant from Us.
[MUQATIL:17:83-84/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The human is an unbeliever: when given provision he turns from supplication and withdraws; when poverty touches him he despairs of good.
[MUQATIL:17:83-84/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The adversity is poverty; when it touches him, he despairs of good.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p158/r4] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The human in this example is a polytheist whom God has granted ease and health.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p158/r5] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The favored person turns away from God.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p158/r6] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid explains naʾā bijānibihi as distancing himself from Us; Yahya says it amounts to the same meaning as turning away.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p158/r7] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The harm that touches him consists of illnesses and hardships.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p158/r8] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · قتادة | reports | Qatada glosses yaʾūs as despairing and losing hope.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p158/r9] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | Yahya says he gives up hope of relief because he has no intention of seeking recompense and no hope.
[FARRA:v2p129/r5] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | When hamza is dropped from يؤوسا, Arabic allows adjacent silent letters; readers instead move the vowel onto wāw, which Farra says is heavier and unattested in ordinary speech. | mentions 2:255, 46:34
[FARRA:v2p129/r6] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | He compares the same treatment with ولا يؤده حفظهما and بعذاب بئيس, where readers move the vowel but Arabic speech retains hamza-less clusters. | mentions 2:255, 46:34
[MAJAZ:v1p389/r3] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | نأى بجانبه means he turned away and withdrew to his side.
[MAJAZ:v1p389/r4] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | يؤسا means profoundly despairing and without hope.
[AKHFASH:v2p426/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | يئوس is derived from يئس.
[TAB-FULL:v15p64/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | After rescue from the sea's danger to shore, a person turns from God's remembrance despite having called on Him alone in distress, acting as if he had never prayed.
[TAB-FULL:v15p64/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Naya bi-janibihi means he turns away from God with his own person, as though he had not previously called on Him in hardship.
[TAB-FULL:v15p64/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid explains the phrase as moving far away from God.
[TAB-FULL:v15p64/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Tabari prefers the eloquent reading with the hamza before the alif; the Medinan reading placing it after the alif is valid Arabic metathesis but less eloquent.
[TAB-FULL:v15p64/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The Medinan reading ناء shifts the hamza as Arabs do in related forms, but it is not the more eloquent language; cited examples illustrate the shift.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p383/r5] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | reports | The readings of wa-naʾā differ in vowel quality and length: Ibn Kathīr and Nāfiʿ open, Ibn ʿĀmir lengthens, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza transmissions vary, and ʿĀṣim and Abū ʿAmr reports differ between this verse and al-Sajda 32:51. | mentions 32:51
[NAHHAS:v2p437/r4] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abū Jaʿfar reads وناء بجانبه; al-Kisāʾī says the forms are dialects, and al-Farrāʾ assigns نأى to the Ḥijāz and ناء to some Hawāzin, Kināna, and most Anṣār.
[NAHHAS:v2p437/r5] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | rejects | Abū Jaʿfar says ناء is metathesized from نأى; the forms نأيت and رأيت show the original order, unlike hypothetical نئت and رئت.
[NAHHAS:v2p437/r6] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الكسائي | reports | For easing the hamza in يؤوسا, al-Kisāʾī transmits يوسا and also cites وإذا المودة, comparing its pronunciation to الموزة.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p220/r2] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Opening nūn and hamza in naʾā preserves the root’s original form, naʾā, on faʿala; the word means to move away.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p220/r3] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Kasra on both nūn and hamza signals the underlying yāʾ by imālah; neighboring vowels draw each other toward kasra, as in shaʿīr and baʿīr.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p220/r4] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Opening nūn but making hamza kasra keeps nūn original and brings hamza toward the neighboring yāʾ; all these forms mean distance, and the noun is al-naʾy.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p220/r5] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Postponing hamza with a lengthened vowel derives nāʾa yanūʾu, to rise while bearing a heavy load; its original wāw became alif, as in the verse about a band of men. | mentions 28:76
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p115#2/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن كثير ونافع | reports | They read naʾā with both nūn and hamza open, in the pattern of naʿā.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p115#2/r10] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | A form with open nūn and kasra hamza leaves the first vowel uninclined, just as an alif is not inclined merely because of a following alif.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p115#2/r11] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | If Abū Bakr's report means kasra on the nūn without hamza imāla, it follows the present-tense pattern yanʾā, by analogy with verbs such as shahida and abā yaʾbā.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p115#2/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن عامر | reports | Ibn ʿĀmir reads nāʾa, like bāʿa.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p115#2/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī have a transmitted form with imāla of the nūn and a kasra on the hamza; another transmission opens the nūn and keeps the hamza kasra.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p115#2/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو بكر عن عاصم | reports | Abū Bakr reports a kasra in this verse, while the hamza is open in al-Sajda. | mentions 32:51
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p115#2/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حفص عن عاصم | reports | Ḥafṣ opens both vowels.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p115#2/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عمرو | reports | Al-Yazīdī and ʿAbd al-Wārith report an open hamza here and in al-Sajda; ʿAbbās reports an imāla-like form glossed as turning aside. | mentions 32:51
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p115#2/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Leaving both fatḥas without imāla is a common Hijazi usage.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p115#2/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Ibn ʿĀmir's form is metathesis; the author compares rāʾa and raʾā and cites a poetic witness.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v5p115#2/r9] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Imāla of the hamza vowel reflects an underlying yāʾ; imāla of the nūn vowel follows it, since speakers may treat a vowel like a letter and incline one vowel because of another.
[SULAMI:v1p395#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | Al-Wasiti says people turn from the Giver through blessings by savoring obedience, enjoying or settling into it, or relying on it for protection; the greatest blessings are guidance, faith, gnosis, and divine friendship.
[THALABI:v6p129/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | When given blessing, a person turns from remembrance and withdraws; when harm touches him, he despairs.
[THALABI:v6p129/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · عطاء | reports | Ata interprets turning away as becoming arrogant and proud.
[THALABI:v6p129/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · القراء | reports | Readers differ on the pronunciation of “ونأى”: Abu Amr, Asim, Nafi, and Hamza in some transmissions use imāla; al-Kisai, Khalaf, and other transmissions of Hamza use kasra; most use fatḥa on both vowels.
[THALABI:v6p129/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو جعفر وعامر | reports | They read it with the nūn form, explained either as a reversal of “نأى” or as deriving from “النوء,” which can mean rising or falling.
[THALABI:v6p129/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | “Harm” means hardship and distress; the person becomes hopeless and despairing.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p268/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | When blessed with health and wealth, a person turns away and distances himself from goodness.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p268/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Alternatively, when given guidance, a person turns away from listening and distances himself from acceptance.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p268/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Nāʾā bi-jānibihi may describe self-admiration, since the conceited shuns people and keeps away from them.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p268/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | It may instead mean distancing oneself from one's Lord.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p268/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Despair of relief after hardship may come from denial and disbelief.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p268/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Alternatively, one despairs because one knows one's sin will bring punishment.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p268/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · قتادة | reports | The affliction here may be poverty.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p268/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الكلبي | reports | It may be illness.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v3p268/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | It may also be the sword.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p454/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas identifies the human as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira; in prosperity he turns aside instead of praying and imploring as he does in affliction.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p454/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مجاهد وابن عباس | reports | Mujahid and Ibn Abbas gloss naʾa bi-janibihi as distancing himself; a report from Mujahid says he moves away from Us, while Ata says it means acting proudly and arrogantly.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p454/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أهل المعاني | reports | The semanticists say he distances himself from fulfilling the rights due for God's blessings; naʾa means distance, as in 6:26, and adds stronger withdrawal to aʿrada. | mentions 6:26
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p454/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The common reading has naʾa with two fatḥas; Ibn Amir reads naʾa with an inverted hamza, like baʿa, a reversal also seen in raʾa/waraʾa and suppor

[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:17:83/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The person meant is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira; when favored he ignores supplication rather than praying fervently as in hardship.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:17:83/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Turning aside means withdrawing from fulfilling the rights due for God's blessings.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:17:83/r3] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The harm is illness or poverty; ya'us means despairing of good and God's mercy because he does not trust God's grace toward His servants.

[DAMGHANI:v1p51/r7] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Al-insān in the verses about turning away after receiving mercy refers to ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa.
[JISHUMI:v6p4286/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Ya'usa is accusative because it is the predicate of kana.
[JISHUMI:v6p4286/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | The composition asks how human turning away after receiving favor connects to the preceding discussion of the Qur'an.
[JISHUMI:v6p4286/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Na'y means distance or turning away; ya's means despair and is synonymous with qunut.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p123#2/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Al-sharr here means hardship and harm; yaʾūsan means despairing and hopeless.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p123#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · قيل | reports | Another reading is that a person prays in distress, but despairs if the answer is delayed; believers should keep praying rather than despair when the answer is late.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p123/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | When God grants a person favor, that person turns away from remembering and calling on God.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p123/r7] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Naʾā bijānibihi means he distances himself, leaving closeness to God through prayer.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p123/r8] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · عطاء | reports | Ata explains the phrase as becoming arrogant and haughty.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p123/r9] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · حمزة والكسائي وأبو بكر وابن عامر وأبو جعفر | reports | Readers vary the vowels in naʾā; Ibn Amir and Abu Jaʿfar read nāʾa like jāʾa, with one view treating it as equivalent to naʾā and another deriving it from rising.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p644#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | When given health and prosperity, a person turns from remembering God as if self-sufficient; turning one's side intensifies the image of arrogance and rejection.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p644#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | When hardship such as poverty, illness, or calamity touches him, he becomes deeply despairing of God's relief.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p644#2/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | The reading wa-nāʾa bi-jānibihi reverses the positions of the root's lām and ʿayn, like rāʾ in raʾā; it can also derive from nāʾ meaning to rise.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p480/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | prefers | The author distinguishes nāʾa as arrogant self-separation from naʾā, distance and departure.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p480/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | When illness, financial loss, or other harm touches them, unbelievers despair because they do not believe in God or trust His control of events.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p480/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | The human may mean unbelievers in particular, using universal phrasing rhetorically; the preceding reference to wrongdoers supports the connection.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p480/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | Alternatively, humanity generally has this blameworthy trait, strongest in unbelievers and present in sinners too.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p480/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet is reported to have said of a believer: he turned away, so God turned away from him.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p480/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Aʿraḍa means turning one’s side away and naʾā means moving far off, depicting abandonment of faith and gratitude.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p480/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن عامر | reports | Ibn ʿAmir alone reads wa-nāʾa; some take it as rising while turned aside, others as a reordered form of naʾā.
[TABRISI:17:82/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Readings of naʾā vary: Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn ʿĀmir via Ibn Dhakwān lengthen and hamzate it; some transmitters use naʾi with a fatḥa then kasra, Ḥamza via al-ʿAjalī, Khalaf, and al-Kisāʾī use kasra on both, and the rest read naʾā.
[TABRISI:17:82/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو علي | reports | Abū ʿAlī analyzes nāʾ as an inverted fāʿil form and cites a poem using rāʾanī as evidence.
[TABRISI:17:82/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Imāla follows because the alif derives from yāʾ in naʾy; readers may incline the first vowel toward the second, while others leave it open.
[TABRISI:17:83/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The statement that supplication only drove them farther away echoes Noah 71:6; alternatively, the Qurʾān exposes their hidden malice and plots against the Prophet. | mentions 71:6
[TABRISI:17:83/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | When granted blessings, a person turns from remembrance as if never to have prayed, then distances himself from gratitude and the duties owed for the blessing.
[TABRISI:17:83/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid reads distancing himself as turning away from God, implying arrogance, self-exaltation, and conceit.
[TABRISI:17:83/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | When hardship, poverty, or affliction strikes, the person despairs instead of patiently hoping for relief, unlike a believer who hopes for relief and mercy.
[TABRISI:17:83/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Although phrased generally, the description specifically concerns unbelievers, who expect no reward for illness and recoil from it; afflictions are truly wise and right.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p80/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | “The human” here is the unbeliever, specifically al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p80/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The blessing is ample provision and removal of affliction.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p80/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, and Ḥafṣ read naʾā with fatḥa on nūn and hamza.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p80/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Ibn ʿĀmir reads nāʾa in the pattern of bāʿa.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p80/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | Al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf from Sulaym from Ḥamza read nāʾa with imāla; Khallād from Sulaym transmits naʾi with a broken hamza.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p80/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Naʾā bi-jānibihi means he distances himself from fulfilling the rights of blessings; another gloss is that he grows proud.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p80/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | When evil—affliction and poverty—touches a person, he becomes deeply despairing and stops hoping for God’s bounty.
[RAZI-FULL:v21p29/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās identifies “the human” as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra; al-Rāzī calls this interpretation far-fetched.
[RAZI-FULL:v21p29/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The person who prospers forgets God, while the deprived person is consumed by grief and also fails to remember God; al-Rāzī compares the pattern with 89:15–16 and 70:19–21. | mentions 89:15, 89:16, 70:19, 70:20, 70:21
[RAZI-FULL:v21p29/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Rāzī instead reads the verse generally: people tend to become arrogant, forget servitude, and rebel against God when they obtain what they want, as 96:6–7 says. | mentions 96:6, 96:7
[RAZI-FULL:v21p29/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Aʿraḍa means he turned away, literally turning his face aside; naʾā bi-jānibihi means he moved far away.
[RAZI-FULL:v21p29/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Moving one’s flank away is an idiom for arrogance, since the arrogant customarily turn aside and present their backs.
[RAZI-FULL:v21p29/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The common reading has fatḥa on both nūn and hamza in naʾā; it is the dominant Arabic form and also occurs in Sūrat Ḥā Mīm al-Sajda. | mentions 41:51
[RAZI-FULL:v21p29/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عامر | reports | Ibn ʿĀmir reads nāʾ; it can reflect metathesis of the word’s final and middle radicals, as in rāʾ for raʾā, or derive from a verb meaning to rise.
[RAZI-FULL:v21p29/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī incline both fatḥas: they incline the hamza and then give the nūn kasra by assimilation to that vowel.
[RAZI-FULL:v21p29/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو عمرو وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي | reports | Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim in Abū Bakr’s narration, and Naṣīr from al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza read naʾā with an open nūn and kasra on the hamza, inclining the hamza.
[RAZI-FULL:v21p29/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The evil that touches a person includes poverty, sickness, or any calamity; then he is intensely despairing of God’s mercy.
[QURTUBI-FULL:17:83/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The people whom Qurʾān increases in loss turn from reflecting on God's signs and are ungrateful for His blessings; one report says the verse was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.
